slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Open by stating that the chapter is not merely about multiplying coordinate columns by a matrix. The central promise is compatibility: the same linear map must move vectors, areas, volumes, dual normals, and inverse images without inventing separate rules for each object. Use the grade ladder to preview the lecture arc and anchor every later formula in this single principle.

slides.label: Subspace Images
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect ordinary linear algebra with the chapter language. A subspace is represented by generators, so the image subspace is obtained by transforming those generators. The important inspection target is the span itself: although the grid shears, the marked one-dimensional subspace remains a straight span through the origin and is now generated by the moved vectors.

slides.label: Outermorphism Rule
slides.notes: Present the outermorphism as a forced construction rather than a new arbitrary operation. The blade is an oriented span built from vector factors, so the honest way to transform it is to move the factors and wedge them again. Point out that this is exactly what preserves degeneracy, orientation, and coordinate independence when students later use matrix representations.

slides.label: Blade Coordinates
slides.notes: Move from the geometric rule to the implementation rule. The wedge construction is primary, but code usually stores coordinates, so we need the correct grade-two matrix. Explain that each bivector coordinate measures a signed projection onto a basis plane. Transforming an area therefore requires all two-by-two minors, which is why simply reusing the vector matrix on blade coordinates would be wrong.

slides.label: Collapse
slides.notes: Use the collapse example to make degeneracy constructive. Students may think a zero blade is a numerical accident, but under a rank-dropping transformation it is exactly the right output. The visual target is the disappearance of area after both transformed generators land on the same line, which ties the algebraic wedge test to geometric dimension loss.

slides.label: Determinant
slides.notes: Reframe determinant away from row operations and toward the top-grade blade. The unit pseudoscalar has no room to rotate inside its own grade, so the outermorphism can only multiply it by a scalar. That scalar is the determinant. Ask students to read magnitude, sign, and zero as volume scale, orientation, and collapse respectively.

slides.label: Orientation
slides.notes: Pause on the sign of the determinant before moving into metric products. The same area magnitude can come from an orientation-preserving or orientation-reversing map, and blades keep that distinction. Use the three panels to ask which ordered pair of transformed vectors agrees with the original traversal and which has been reflected.

slides.label: Adjoint
slides.notes: After the metric-free outer product, introduce the first place where measurements need extra care. The adjoint is not a mysterious transpose trick; it is the bookkeeping map that moves a linear transformation from the object being measured to the measuring object. This prepares students for normals, contractions, and dual descriptions that cannot be pushed forward like ordinary tangent vectors.

slides.label: Dual Normals
slides.notes: Make this slide concrete by naming the programming error it prevents. Surface tangents are direct objects, so their bivector transforms by the outermorphism. The normal is the dual measurement that annihilates those tangents, so it must transform by the determinant times inverse transpose rule. Ask students to check perpendicularity against both transformed tangent directions.

slides.label: Contraction
slides.notes: Use the commuting diagram to show why contraction is the chapter's first genuinely metric-sensitive operation. Students already know the outer product transforms by moving factors. Contraction compares a vector with a blade using the metric, so the comparison vector must be adjusted by the inverse adjoint when the blade is transformed. The diagram gives two paths to the same vector result.

slides.label: Inverse Maps
slides.notes: Make the inverse map feel grade-wise, not merely vector-wise. If the vector map has an inverse, then applying the inverse to each transformed generator rebuilds the original blade. The formula involving exterior powers is the matrix version of that statement. Mention that this is also why singular maps are special: once a blade is collapsed, no inverse blade can recover the lost dimension.

slides.label: Implementation
slides.notes: Translate the chapter into an implementation ledger. A multivector library may store arrays and matrices, but each grade must receive the matrix that matches its geometric meaning. The best sanity check is composition: transforming by M and then N should agree with the exterior power of the product. This detects many subtle basis-order and sign mistakes.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by giving students a practical debugging checklist. The chapter's ideas become useful when a transformed subspace, area, volume, or normal looks suspicious in code. Walk through the four questions and emphasize that each one is geometric: rebuild from transformed generators, use the correct grade matrix, check signed top-grade scaling, and treat dual measurements with the inverse adjoint.
